Insomuch
in-so-MUCH
conjunction
A compacted phrase, in so much, from Old English in + swa + micel; hence “to such a degree,” “so much so that” — a conjunction of consequence, introducing the effect that followed.

Biblical Definition

Insomuch is the Authorized Version’s conjunction of consequence: it means to such a degree that, and it always points forward to a result. It must be carefully distinguished from its near neighbour inasmuch, which points backward to a reason. Where the AV says insomuch that, it is measuring an effect: the thing was so great that this followed. So the multitude sees the dumb speak and the lame walk, “Insomuch that the multitude wondered… and they glorified the God of Israel” (Mat 15:31). So the palsied man rises with his bed, “insomuch that they were all amazed, and glorified God” (Mar 2:12). So the apostolic power in Jerusalem was such that the sick were laid in the streets for Peter’s shadow (Act 5:15). The little word is therefore a measuring-rod laid against the works of God, and the reader who skips it loses the writer’s emphasis. It measures evil as well: the dissembling at Antioch went so far that “Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation” (Gal 2:13) — the hypocrisy was of such a degree that even a good man, the son of consolation who had fetched Saul from Tarsus, was swept along. And the Lord warns of deceivers whose signs shall be such that, were it possible, they should deceive the very elect. Insomuch asks the reader to stop and take the measure of the thing described, whether mercy or madness.

Webster 1828 Definition

So that; to such a degree that — a conjunction introducing the consequence or effect.

expand to see more

INSOMUCH, so that; to such a degree; used to introduce a consequence.

A compacting of the phrase in so much — in so great a measure.

It always looks forward to an effect, never backward to a cause.

Distinguish from inasmuch, which gives a reason: seeing that, because.

The healings were such, insomuch that the multitude wondered (Mat 15:31).

Key Scripture

Mat 15:31 — "Insomuch that the multitude wondered, when they saw the dumb to speak, the maimed to be whole, the lame to walk, and the blind to see: and they glorified the God of Israel."

Mar 2:12 — "And immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went forth before them all; insomuch that they were all amazed, and glorified God, saying, We never saw it on this fashion."

Act 5:15 — "Insomuch that they brought forth the sick into the streets, and laid them on beds and couches, that at the least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them."

Gal 2:13 — "And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation."

Modern Corruption

No modern movement has redefined a conjunction; the loss is that readers now skim the very words by which Scripture measures its own wonders.

expand to see more

The live danger is not redefinition but blindness. Modern reading habits move fast, and the small connectives of the Authorized Version are the first casualties. A reader who does not know that insomuch introduces a consequence, and that inasmuch introduces a reason, will glide over both and lose the shape of the argument. Worse, he will confuse them, and confusion between a reason and a result is the seed of a great many bad readings — the classic case being Mat 25:40, where inasmuch is regularly heard as though it were insomuch, turning a stated ground of judgment into a supposed effect of good works. Scripture is written tightly; the Spirit gave the joints as well as the bones. To read the Bible for its stirring phrases while skipping its logic is to read it as a devotional scrapbook rather than as the word of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the old Protestant habit of grammatical reading: God has spoken in real sentences, and the sense of a sentence is carried as much by that, therefore, insomuch, wherefore as by its nouns. The Reformers built the recovery of the gospel on exactly such reading — Luther on a Greek preposition, the whole doctrine of imputation resting on how a clause is joined. Every place the AV says insomuch that, it is inviting wonder: look how far this went. The multitude wondered and glorified the God of Israel; a paralytic walked out through the crowd; and, on the darker side, even Barnabas was carried away. Read the joints, and the wonder and the warning both land where the Spirit aimed them.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means “to such a degree that” — it introduces a consequence.

expand to see more

Insomuch — a compacting of in so much, in so great a measure.

It is a conjunction of RESULT: the thing was so great that this followed.

Inasmuch is its opposite number, a conjunction of REASON: seeing that, because.

The AV uses it to measure mercy (Mat 15:31; Mar 2:12; Act 5:15).

It also measures evil: the dissembling reached even Barnabas (Gal 2:13).

Usage

"Insomuch that = so much so that; it names the effect, never the reason."

"Do not confuse insomuch with inasmuch: one gives the result, the other the ground."

"Where the AV says insomuch, it is asking the reader to take the measure of the thing."
